title: Putting the 'renew’ into renewables | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie argues that more than 70% of the world's 3.5 TW of wind and solar capacity will face a decommission, extend or repower decision in the 2040s, and that repowering is economically compelling because it reuses grid connections and permits while capturing large technology gains. Equipment suppliers are the biggest winners, with global equipment sales potentially more than 60% higher in 2050 than today even as net additions slow.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie forecasts that over 70% of the more than 3.5 TW of wind and solar capacity operating worldwide by end-2025 will face a decommission, life-extension or repowering decision in the 2040s.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Creates a multi-terawatt replacement market independent of new greenfield demand.
insights.locator: How big is the decommissioning challenge?

insights.claim: Almost 50 GW of global wind capacity is now over 20 years old, roughly the design life of early turbines, rising to over 230 GW by 2040, and solar capacity older than 20 years will overtake wind before 2040.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Wind repowering is the near-term opportunity; solar follows in the late 2030s.
insights.locator: Ageing wind projects are the most pressing

insights.claim: Decommissioning will drive 44% of wind and almost a quarter of solar buildout worldwide in the 2040s, with even higher shares in established markets across Europe, Asia and the Americas.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Mature markets' renewable demand will increasingly be replacement-driven.

insights.claim: Repowering has capital and operating costs on par with greenfield projects, so its advantage comes mainly from higher output from newer technology, plus the ability to skip grid-connection queues and often clear permitting faster.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Existing sites with grid interconnection are valuable assets given connection-queue bottlenecks.
insights.quote: Given the site will always outlast the equipment, repowered projects can also skip grid-connection queues and often clear permitting faster.

insights.claim: In Germany, decommissioned wind sites have average wind speeds 4% higher than new greenfield projects, delivering higher capacity factors and lower levelised cost of energy when repowered.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Early-deployed sites occupy the best resource, favoring owners of legacy portfolios.

insights.claim: Without repowering, growth in global annual wind and solar installations risks stalling as policy support softens, requiring more coal and gas to fill the gap.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Repowering policy is a swing factor for future thermal generation demand.
insights.locator: And it isn’t only about economics

insights.claim: Average wind turbine ratings have increased fourfold over two decades, solar module efficiency has risen almost 70%, and solar sites now need about a third less land for the same capacity.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Same footprint can host far more capacity, boosting repowered site output.

insights.claim: Wind turbine design life has climbed from 20 years to more than 30, and solar panel warranties have lengthened by five years as degradation improves.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Longer asset lives improve project economics and delay future replacement cycles.
insights.locator: Hardware is also getting more robust

themes.theme: Implications for targets and power prices

insights.claim: Meeting the European Commission's 500 GW wind target for 2030 requires about 37 GW of additions a year, and if all end-of-design-life projects are decommissioned rather than repowered, around 2 GW more per year would be needed.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Retirements make EU wind targets harder, supporting repowering-friendly policy.
insights.locator: Simply decommissioning ageing wind and solar

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie estimates repowering existing German onshore wind projects would raise the country's onshore wind output 16% in 2050, equal to almost a third of Germany's current annual wind generation, and could significantly lower power prices.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Repowering is a deflationary force on European power prices.

insights.claim: Repowering could make global wind and solar equipment sales more than 60% higher in 2050 than today even as annual net capacity additions decline, making equipment suppliers the biggest beneficiaries alongside consumers.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Supports a long-duration replacement demand thesis for turbine and module OEMs.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie argues repowering could usher in an era with more wind and solar installations than ever, and that planning for renewal should already be on the agenda amid volatile fossil fuel prices.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Strategic positioning for repowering pipelines is relevant to capital allocation now.
insights.quote: Repowering could usher in an era of renewal and lead to more wind and solar installations than ever before.
insights.locator: Repowering could usher in an era
